sourcesNote: Lewes descriptions and current visitor information are based primarily on Visit Lewes and Sussex Past; opening information is deliberately treated as provisional and should be refreshed from official sources before a real visit.

stops.title: Lewes Castle and Barbican
stops.text: Lewes Castle is the most obvious reminder that the town was reshaped after the Norman Conquest. William de Warenne built a motte-and-bailey castle here soon after 1066, and the site was developed over the following centuries. What you see today is unusual because the castle has two surviving mottes: the main keep mound and the Brack Mount, with the Barbican forming the later defensive entrance. The climb is steep, so for a gentle walking tour we treat the interior as optional. Even from below, the castle explains Lewes's geography: the Norman stronghold dominates the medieval town and commands the surrounding valley. If you do climb, the reward is a broad view over the town and the South Downs. The nearby Barbican House Museum adds archaeological context, but the outdoor viewpoint is enough to make the castle one of the tour's key stops.
stops.tip: The castle climb is steep and includes stairs. Exterior viewing is much easier.

stops.title: Anne of Cleves House
stops.text: This timber-framed house is one of Lewes's most evocative Tudor buildings. It dates from the fifteenth century and became associated with Anne of Cleves because the house formed part of the settlement granted to her after her short marriage to Henry VIII. The important qualification is that Anne never actually lived here. Inside, the rooms illustrate domestic life rather than royal grandeur: a Tudor kitchen, parlour and bedroom help turn a familiar name from the history books into something tangible. The garden continues the theme with plants appropriate to Tudor life. For our walking tour the exterior is still worthwhile if the museum is closed, because the timber framing and irregular medieval form are easy to appreciate from Southover High Street. The house is one of Sussex Past's three major historic sites in Lewes.
stops.tip: Flat approach. Interior is stair-accessed and should be treated as optional.
stops.coordSource: Anne of Cleves House — Historic England/OpenStreetMap

stops.title: Lewes Priory and Priory Park
stops.text: Lewes Priory was founded by William de Warenne and his wife Gundrada between 1078 and 1082. It became one of the most important Cluniac monasteries in England, and its buildings once occupied a large area of Southover. The Dissolution of the Monasteries in the sixteenth century brought the religious community to an end, after which much of the stone was reused elsewhere. Today the surviving fragments are set in Priory Park, where interpretation panels help reconstruct the vanished complex. The site is also tied to one of Lewes's defining historical episodes: after the Battle of Lewes in 1264, King Henry III surrendered at the priory. Unlike the castle, this is a largely level outdoor stop, making it particularly suitable for a gentle walking tour. Allow yourself time to look at the scale of the ruins and imagine how much larger the medieval complex once was.
stops.tip: Mostly level and suitable for a gentle walk. Outdoor site.
stops.coordSource: Lewes Priory/Priory Park — Lewes Priory Trust

stops.title: Southover Grange Gardens
stops.text: Southover Grange Gardens provide a welcome change of pace. The gardens belonged to the grange built in 1542 by William Newton and were later associated with the diarist John Evelyn. Today the walled garden is a public space divided by the Winterbourne stream, with quiet corners, a fountain, a disused well and planting that gives the centre of Lewes a surprisingly secluded feel. It is useful on a walking tour because it shows another side of the town's history: not castles and battles, but the way large houses, gardens and water shaped everyday life. It also gives us a chance to slow down. If you have only half an hour in Lewes, this may not beat the castle or priory; with an hour or more, it is an excellent low-effort addition.
stops.tip: Level and restful. A good stop if you want less history and more atmosphere.

stops.title: High Street — the medieval town spine
stops.text: Lewes High Street is best understood as a landscape rather than a single building. The street follows the historic spine of the town, climbing gently between the medieval centre and the castle. Look at the mixture of timber framing, Georgian fronts, shop windows, inns and narrow side passages. Lewes's survival as a small county town has left an unusually rich concentration of older buildings. The street also demonstrates how history is still part of ordinary life: independent shops occupy buildings whose proportions and plots can be centuries old. From here, the castle rises above you and the routes towards Southover and the Priory lead downhill. This makes the High Street an excellent orientation zone. Rather than stopping at one exact doorway, take a few minutes to look in both directions and compare the changing scale and age of the buildings.
stops.tip: Mostly level along the central section, though the street rises towards the castle.
stops.coordSource: Lewes High Street — OS/Open Postcode street reference

stops.title: Lewes Town Hall and Market Square
stops.text: The Town Hall area is a useful place to pause because it connects Lewes's civic life with its commercial history. The town has long functioned as the administrative centre of the county and as a market town serving the surrounding villages. From the square, look at the layers around you: civic buildings, shops, older houses and routes leading towards the castle and the lower town. Lewes also has a long tradition of local independence, something that remains visible today in its strong independent shopping culture and even its own local currency, the Lewes Pound. This is not a stop where one building tells the whole story. Instead, it is a chance to understand Lewes as a living town whose historic centre still performs the same basic jobs it did in earlier centuries: meeting, trading, governing and passing through.
stops.tip: Level square; good place to orientate yourself and rest.

stops.title: Keere Street — a medieval lane
stops.text: Keere Street is one of the places where Lewes's medieval street pattern becomes tangible. The narrow lane connects the upper town with Southover and is lined with old houses, shops and walls. It is picturesque, but it is also a reminder that medieval streets were designed around pedestrians, carts and property boundaries rather than modern traffic. The gradient is the reason we treat it as an optional section for a gentle tour. If you are comfortable with a short hill, the lane is rewarding because the changing views make the town feel much older than its modern shops suggest. If you prefer flat walking, the app can bypass it without losing the main historical story.
stops.tip: Steep section. Optional for a gentle tour; bypass if desired.

stops.title: Harvey's Brewery and Cliffe High Street
stops.text: Harvey's Brewery is one of Lewes's most distinctive modern continuities. The brewery describes itself as the oldest independent brewery in Sussex, and the Harvey family has been associated with the business since 1790. The brewery stands beside the River Ouse in the Cliffe area, where the town's commercial life historically connected to river transport and trade. You cannot reproduce the experience of a working brewery simply by looking at the outside, but the buildings and the smell of brewing can make the history unusually immediate. Cliffe High Street itself is worth seeing as a separate part of Lewes: it has a strong independent character and a different feel from the more formal upper High Street. This is an especially good stop if you want the tour to include the town's continuing identity rather than only its medieval past.
stops.tip: Level. Brewery tours are separate; exterior and shop are enough for the walking guide.

stops.title: Cliffe High Street and the Ouse
stops.text: Cliffe occupies the lower eastern side of Lewes beside the River Ouse. Historically this was an important commercial area, and the river helped connect Lewes with the wider Sussex economy. Today the area is one of the best places to experience the town's independent shops and everyday atmosphere. Look for the way the street falls towards the river and notice how different the architecture feels from the castle quarter. This is also a useful place to understand why Lewes developed where it did: the river, the crossing point and the defensible high ground all contributed to the town's importance. The app treats the whole area as a zone rather than asking you to stand at a single doorway, because the story makes more sense when you can see the street, river and hillside together.
stops.tip: Level and spacious by Lewes standards.
stops.coordSource: Cliffe High Street — postcode/OpenStreetMap street reference

stops.title: St Anne's Church and the old churchyard
stops.text: St Anne's Church stands in one of the quieter historic corners of central Lewes. The churchyard is particularly valuable for the walking tour because it provides a sense of how closely medieval and later communities lived around their parish churches. The church itself has medieval origins, while the surrounding town contains buildings from many later periods. Pause here and look back towards the High Street and castle. Lewes is compact, but its hills and lanes create a sequence of distinct neighbourhoods. A churchyard such as this acts as a small green interruption in that urban pattern. It is also a useful reminder that the town's history is not just the story of rulers and battles: parish churches were places where ordinary people worshipped, were married, buried their dead and organised community life for centuries.
stops.tip: Level approach and a quiet place to pause.
stops.coordSource: St Anne's Church — Historic England/geotagged reference

stops.title: Bull House — Thomas Paine
stops.text: Bull House is associated with Thomas Paine, the radical writer and political thinker who spent part of his early life in Lewes. Paine became one of the most influential political pamphleteers of the eighteenth century, later writing Common Sense and The Rights of Man. The Lewes connection matters because the town's tradition of independent political thought predates Paine and continued long afterwards. From the outside, Bull House is simply another historic building in the centre; the significance comes from the person associated with it. This is a good example of why the City Guides repertoire needs more places than a normal tour can include. If you have plenty of time and enjoy political history, it is an excellent stop. If you have only thirty minutes, the app can leave it out while retaining the castle, priory and historic centre.
stops.tip: Flat and short stop; exterior only.

stops.title: Westgate and the old town entrance
stops.text: Westgate marks one of the historic approaches to Lewes. Gates like this controlled movement through medieval towns, and the survival of the name helps us reconstruct the older shape of Lewes even where the original defences have disappeared. The town's position mattered: the Ouse valley offered trade and communication, while the higher ground around the castle provided defence. Standing at Westgate, look along the street and imagine the much more restricted town entrance that medieval travellers would have encountered. It is also a useful point for understanding how the modern road network has inherited the older street pattern. This is a small stop, so it is particularly suitable for a short tour or as a link between the upper town and other sights.
stops.coordSource: Westgate Chapel / historic West Gate area — Historic England/OpenStreetMap

stops.title: Pells Pool and the riverside
stops.text: Pells Pool is a reminder that Lewes has a life beyond its monuments. The outdoor swimming pool is described locally as the world's oldest freshwater public swimming pool still in use. Whether or not you are interested in swimming, the site helps explain the relationship between Lewes and its watercourses. The town sits in the Ouse valley, and streams and springs have always influenced its landscape. This is therefore a good optional stop for a relaxed tour: it gives you a break from buildings and offers a glimpse of a more everyday aspect of local life. It also helps demonstrate why a good city guide should not consist entirely of famous monuments. Interesting places can explain a city's character even when they are not its headline attractions.
stops.tip: Flat riverside stop; seasonal opening is separate from the walking tour.

stops.title: Lewes Railway Station and modern arrival
stops.text: Lewes Railway Station is included for a practical reason as well as a historical one: it demonstrates that the town can be entered from many directions. The station links Lewes with Brighton, Eastbourne, Hastings and London, and it is close enough to the historic centre to make an excellent alternative starting point for the guide. The railway changed the way people reached Lewes in the nineteenth century, making the town less dependent on road and river transport. For City Guides, this stop is also a test of the idea that a tour should not assume a cruise ship or tourist office as its starting point. If you begin here, press I AM HERE and the app should build a worthwhile tour from the station rather than sending you first to a predetermined Stop 1.
stops.tip: Flat and useful as a starting point. Excellent GPS test location.

stops.title: Battle of Lewes — the 1264 story
stops.text: Lewes is unusually important in the history of medieval constitutional conflict because of the Battle of Lewes on 14 May 1264. Simon de Montfort and his rebel barons defeated the forces of King Henry III and Prince Edward. The victory led to the Mise of Lewes, an attempt to force the king to accept constraints on royal government, and the episode is often remembered in Lewes as part of the long development of parliamentary government. The battlefield itself lies beyond the compact centre, so this guide uses a broad story zone rather than pretending that one modern street corner is the battlefield. The castle and priory provide the strongest physical links to the event: the castle was the dominant stronghold, while the priory became the place where Henry III ultimately surrendered. If your time is short, hearing this story at either site is more useful than making a special detour.
stops.tip: Use as a story zone near the historic centre; the full battlefield lies outside the gentle town circuit.
stops.coordSource: Battle of Lewes interpretation marker at castle — geotagged historical marker
